open_questions.q: Exactly how do the first few particles come together to start a crystal?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can watch crystals grow, but the very first moment is too small and fast to see well. Some think particles first gather in a loose cloud and only then line up. It is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do two salt crystals in the same glass sometimes grow different-looking faces, such as hollow, stepped cubes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that edges can grow faster than the middle of a face when the water is very full of salt. Predicting the exact shape of any one crystal is still very hard.

open_questions.q: How do living bodies build crystals exactly where they need them, such as in teeth and in the ear?
open_questions.why_open: Biologists know that proteins guide where the crystals grow and what shape they take. Many of the details are still not known.

open_questions.q: Are there crystal patterns that nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: New kinds of crystals are still being made in laboratories and found in rocks and meteorites. Nobody knows how many more there are.

maths.context: This is about the Fast Plate or Slow Glass test. You measured the biggest crystal from each dish.
maths.problem: Meenakshi's biggest plate crystal was 1 millimetre across. Her biggest glass crystal was 6 millimetres across. How many plate crystals, lined up side by side, would reach across the glass crystal?
maths.explain: 6 divided by 1 is 6. So 6 tiny plate crystals in a row are as wide as one glass crystal.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two sizes as 'how many fit across' shows how big the difference really is.

maths.context: This is about how a salt crystal grows. A salt cube is built like a stack of tiny cubes.
maths.problem: A small salt cube is 2 tiny blocks long, 2 wide and 2 high. How many tiny blocks is it made of? If it grows to 3 blocks long, 3 wide and 3 high, how many blocks then?
maths.explain: One layer of 2 by 2 is 4 blocks. Two layers make 8. One layer of 3 by 3 is 9 blocks. Three layers make 27. So growing just one block wider on each side more than triples the number of blocks.
maths.why_maths: Counting layers shows why a crystal needs far more particles to grow even a little bigger, which is why big crystals take so long.

maths.context: This is about the faces of a salt crystal. A salt crystal is a cube, like a dice.
maths.problem: How many faces, edges and corners does a salt cube have? Nila finds 4 salt cubes stuck together in a row. How many faces of the row can you see from outside?
maths.answer: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners. A row of 4 has 18 faces showing.
maths.explain: Each cube has 6 faces, so 4 cubes have 24. Where two cubes touch, 2 faces are hidden, one on each. A row of 4 has 3 joins, so 3 times 2 is 6 faces hidden. 24 take away 6 is 18.
maths.why_maths: Counting faces, edges and corners is how scientists describe a crystal's shape exactly.

maths.context: This is about the Grow Your Own Kalkandu project. You measured the biggest crystal on the thread every few days.
maths.problem: Shruti measured her biggest sugar crystal. Day 3: 1 millimetre. Day 5: 3 millimetres. Day 7: 5 millimetres. If it keeps growing the same way, how big will it be on day 9? Why might it slow down later?
maths.answer: About 7 millimetres on day 9. It may slow down because the syrup has less sugar left to give.
maths.explain: It grows 2 millimetres every 2 days: 1, 3, 5, so next is 7. But each crystal takes sugar out of the syrup. As the syrup holds less spare sugar, growth slows unless more water evaporates.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict, and then the real crystal tests your prediction.

roots.context: We have grown salt crystals fast and slowly, and seen that each substance grows its own shape. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your plate dried fast and grew many tiny salt grains. Your glass dried slowly and grew fewer, bigger ones. Under the lens, both had flat faces and square corners. The drying speed set their size, but the salt itself set their shape.
deep_truth.habit: We think a neat shape must be made from outside, by a mould, a knife or a maker's hands. Salt makes its own cubes, because its particles always join in the same square pattern.
deep_truth.evidence: In the plate and glass test, the size changed but both made cubes. Cracked kal uppu broke into smaller blocks. Phitkari and sugar each grew their own different shape, in the same kind of glass.

three.who_am_i: Your body grows crystals too. The enamel on your teeth is made of tiny crystals that your body built from the calcium in your food.
three.what_is_life: Your body needs to know which way is down, even with your eyes shut. Inside each ear, tiny crystals rest on a soft jelly. When you tilt your head, they shift, and tiny hairs feel it.
three.what_is_this_world: Most rocks, most metals, sand, snow and the salt in the sea are made of crystals. Much of the solid world grew itself, particle by particle.

roots.thread: A salt crystal starts with a few particles that join and stay. Every particle that follows joins in the same way, millions of times over. Out of that one way of joining come the cubes on your plate, the heaps at Thoothukudi and the rock salt from old dried seas. One simple pattern shows up as countless crystals, big and small, in every place where salt water dries.

teachings.teaching: A tree as wide as your arms can reach grows from a tiny shoot. A tower nine storeys high starts from a heap of earth. A journey of a thousand miles starts beneath your feet.
teachings.link: Your biggest crystal grew the same way, one tiny particle at a time, over days. The slow glass shows that big things need many small steps, not a rush.

teachings.teaching: Plato, a Greek thinker, guessed that each of the elements is made of tiny shapes. He gave earth the cube, because it is the steadiest shape.
teachings.link: Plato was wrong about the elements. But he was right that tiny shapes, repeated, can build the things we see. Salt really is cube-shaped, because of the way its particles join.

science.text: The shape of a crystal comes from the way its particles are arranged. X-rays shone through crystals since 1912 show the arrangement.
Exactly how the first few particles come together to start a crystal is still being studied.

other_view.view: Saying the salt 'sets its own shape' is just a way of describing the forces between its particles. The forces are what we measure. The cube follows from them, and nothing more is needed to explain it.

practice.title: Watch a crystal face
practice.say: Hold one big salt crystal or a piece of kalkandu near the window. Turn it slowly until one face catches the light and shines. Keep it still there. Breathe in and out slowly five times. With each breath, picture one more row of particles joining that face. Now put it down. Your crystal grew without hurrying. Open your hands.
practice.kid: Hold a crystal near the window. Turn it until one face shines. Keep it still. Breathe slowly five times. Picture one more row joining with each breath.

ask: Nobody shaped your salt cubes. Where do you think their shape came from?
Is a crystal that grew for a week more special than one that grew in an hour? Why?
Your body grows crystals in your teeth and ears. Did you make them, or did they make themselves?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today. The plate and glass test uses one cup of water and about 5 big spoons of salt, which every kitchen has. Two big spoons spread on a plate dry in a few hours to a day on an indoor shelf. The same amount in a narrow glass is about 1 to 2 centimetres deep and takes about 5 to 7 days, and grows cubes a few millimetres across, which a ruler and a phone camera show clearly. The step notes say what to do if the glass grows only small crystals. Phitkari is sold cheaply in most Indian towns, and dissolves in hot water and grows crystals overnight as it cools. The adult handles hot water and hot syrup. The kalkandu project has a fix for syrup that is too weak, and an ant moat. Cracking kal uppu uses a spoon pressed slowly, not a hammer. The frost hunt is outside the spine, because not every fridge has frost. The spine is about 85 minutes, with the glass checked on later days for 5 minutes at a time.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that every crystal of one kind follows the same rule? This card tells how.
how_we_found_out.who: Nicolas Steno, a Danish doctor and scientist who worked in Florence, Italy
how_we_found_out.when: 1669, with more measuring in France in the 1770s and 1780s
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Crystals of one kind can grow in any shape, because no two look alike.
how_we_found_out.story: Clear quartz, called rock crystal, has been collected for thousands of years. No two pieces look alike. Some are long and thin, some short and fat, some lopsided. So it seemed that crystals of one kind could grow in any shape, with no rule. In 1669, Nicolas Steno, a Danish doctor working in Florence, Italy, looked more carefully. He studied many quartz crystals and drew their outlines when cut across. The faces were of every size. But when he compared the angle between one face and the next, it was the same in every crystal. A lopsided crystal had the same angles as a neat one. Only the sizes of the faces had changed. Steno also wrote that a crystal grows by adding new layers to its outside, from the liquid around it. About a hundred years later, scientists in France measured many kinds of crystals with a new tool for measuring angles. Each kind had its own fixed angles. Today we know why. The particles in each kind of crystal always join in the same pattern.
